lead: Specific heat is the heat needed to raise 1 kg of a gas by 1 K. At constant volume the heat per kg goes only into internal energy, so q = cv ΔT. At constant pressure the gas also expands and does pΔv work, so q = cp ΔT and cp is larger. For an ideal gas cp − cv = R. Only a few universities teach this as a separate topic, but these numbers size compressors, engine cylinders and air-conditioning coils.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.2 for u, h and Δh = cpΔT.

blocks.text: cv is the specific heat at constant volume: cv = (∂u/∂T) at fixed v. It is the heat per kg per kelvin that raises internal energy when volume is fixed. cp is the specific heat at constant pressure: cp = (∂h/∂T) at fixed p. It is the heat per kg per kelvin that raises enthalpy when pressure is fixed. Both have units kJ/kg·K. For an ideal gas u and h depend only on T, so du = cv dT and dh = cp dT.

blocks.where: u and h are specific internal energy and enthalpy in kJ/kg; T is temperature in K; subscripts v and p mean volume or pressure held fixed.

blocks.text: In a rigid closed vessel no boundary moves, so w = 0 and Q = ΔU = m cv ΔT. In a piston at constant pressure the gas expands and does pΔv work. The same ΔT then needs extra heat: Q = ΔH = m cp ΔT.
For 1 kg of ideal gas, pΔv = RΔT. The first law gives cpΔT = cvΔT + RΔT, so cp − cv = R. At constant volume every kilojoule of heat stays in the gas; at constant pressure part leaves as work.

Mayer's relation is cp − cv = R. R is the gas constant in kJ/kg·K. The specific heat ratio γ = cp/cv is dimensionless. Kinetic theory gives γ = 1 + 2/f, where f is degrees of freedom; use this only as a memory aid.
cp − cv = R, γ = cp/cv, cv = R/(γ − 1), cp = γR/(γ − 1)
blocks.where: cp and cv are in kJ/kg·K; R is in kJ/kg·K; γ is dimensionless.

blocks.text: Standard values: monatomic gases γ ≈ 1.67, diatomic gases such as air γ ≈ 1.4, polyatomic gases γ ≈ 1.3. For air at about 300 K: cp = 1.005, cv = 0.718, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K. At high temperature cp rises, so use gas tables for large temperature ranges.
Use cv for a rigid tank and cp for a constant-pressure heater. For a nozzle or turbine, cpΔT still gives Δh for an ideal gas. Chapter 2.4 uses γ in pV^γ = C.

figure.caption: At constant volume all heat raises internal energy; at constant pressure part of the heat does pΔv work. For air the gap is R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, so cp is larger than cv.

spec.title: Same temperature rise, different heat
spec.aria: The same temperature rise needs less heat at constant volume than at constant pressure, and the difference is R.

examples.question: Air has cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K and cv = 0.718 kJ/kg·K. Find R and γ. Check R using M = 28.97 kg/kmol and Ru = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K.
steps: For an ideal gas, R = cp − cv = 1.005 − 0.718 = 0.287 kJ/kg·K.
The molar check uses R = Ru/M, with M = 28.97 kg/kmol.
The two R values agree to three decimals; any 0.001 difference is rounding.
examples.answer: R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, γ = 1.40, and the molar check also gives R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K.
examples.check:
cp = 1.005
cv = 0.718
R = cp - cv
gamma = cp / cv
M = 28.97
Ru = 8.314
R_molar = Ru / M
print(round(R, 3))
print(round(gamma, 3))
print(round(R_molar, 3))

traps: Using cp in a rigid vessel at constant volume. For air this overestimates Q by γ ≈ 1.4, about 40%.
Mixing R = 287 J/kg·K with cp and cv in kJ/kg·K. Convert R to 0.287 kJ/kg·K first.
Using air's cp and cv for every gas. R and γ depend on the gas.
Treating cp and cv as constant over a large temperature range. They rise with T; use tables.
Applying cp − cv = R to a real gas near saturation or to a liquid. It is an ideal-gas relation.

quiz.q: Define cv and cp. Give their units.
Why is cp greater than cv for a gas?
quiz.a: At constant pressure the gas expands and does pΔv work, so more heat is needed for the same ΔT.

quiz.q: 2 kg of air is heated 20 K in a rigid tank. Take cv = 0.718 kJ/kg·K. Find Q.
0.5 kg of air is heated 40 K at constant pressure. Take cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K. Find Q.
A student uses cp instead of cv for a rigid tank of air. By what factor is Q overestimated?
quiz.a: The wrong Q is cp/cv = γ ≈ 1.4 times the correct Q, so 40% too high.

quiz.q: Give γ for monatomic gases, diatomic air and polyatomic gases.
Why is cp − cv = R true for an ideal gas?
quiz.a: For 1 kg of ideal gas pΔv = RΔT. Constant-pressure heat adds this work to the constant-volume heat, giving cp − cv = R.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real gases have cp and cv that change with temperature, so engine and turbine calculations use polynomial fits or gas tables. Compressor and IC-engine codes call these polynomials many times per cycle. HVAC design uses cp of moist air, and high-speed flow uses γ. Search for ideal gas specific heat tables or NASA 7-coefficient polynomials.
